results.key_finding: DaTscan reliably distinguishes presynaptic dopaminergic neurodegenerative disorders (PD, MSA, PSP) — which yield an abnormal scan — from essential tremor, drug-induced parkinsonism, and psychogenic tremor — which yield a normal scan. Sensitivity and specificity for detecting dopaminergic deficit exceed 90% in multicenter studies.
results.title: DaTscan (Ioflupane I-123 SPECT) for differentiating Parkinson's disease from non-degenerative tremor disorders including essential tremor

results.key_finding: Clinically established PD requires bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity, with supportive criteria including levodopa response and olfactory loss. Essential tremor is a recognized mimic; the key discriminator is the presence of bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity in PD (absent in pure ET) and, when uncertain, abnormal DaTscan (normal in ET, abnormal in PD).
results.title: MDS Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for Parkinson's Disease

results.key_finding: Features that distinguish PD from ET include: asymmetric rest tremor (re-emergent pattern), cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, micrographia, reduced arm swing, and positive Myerson sign. ET is characterized by bilateral symmetric postural/kinetic tremor, alcohol responsiveness, and a positive family history — none of which exclude PD. DaTscan is the recommended ancillary test when clinical uncertainty exists; it is normal in pure ET regardless of family history or alcohol response.
results.title: Distinguishing essential tremor from Parkinson's disease: clinical features, DaTscan, and treatment response

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Gerald Hartmann is a 64-year-old right-handed retired civil engineer who is referred to the neurology outpatient clinic by his primary care physician for evaluation of a new resting tremor in his right hand. He has a well-established, 20-year history of bilateral postural and action tremor that was diagnosed as essential tremor by his primary care physician in his mid-forties. This tremor has been largely stable and well controlled on propranolol 40 mg twice daily. He has noted throughout his life that one to two alcoholic drinks reliably and noticeably reduce the tremor — a feature his father and brother, who both have similar shaking, have also observed.

Approximately 10 months ago, his wife first noticed a new quality to his right-hand tremor: a slow, rhythmic trembling that occurred when his hand was resting in his lap while watching television, which was distinctly different from the postural tremor she had observed for years. The patient initially attributed this to a worsening of his essential tremor. Over the subsequent months, however, he has developed progressive stiffness and slowness affecting primarily the right side of his body. He finds it more difficult to button his shirt with his right hand, his right arm does not swing when he walks, and his handwriting has become smaller and less legible.

He also reports increased difficulty with fine manipulation tasks in his model railroading hobby, particularly with small parts requiring right-hand dexterity. His wife has noted that he occasionally seems to 'freeze' at the start of walking, and that he appears generally slower in all activities. He has had two near-falls while turning quickly over the past four months. He denies falls to the ground, visual hallucinations, cognitive decline, or urinary incontinence. He reports mild constipation over the past year, which he manages with dietary fiber. His wife has noted that he occasionally talks softly and moves his limbs during sleep over the past 8 months, which he was previously not doing.

The patient is concerned that he may simply have a worsening of his essential tremor, noting the strong family history of tremor (father, brother, maternal aunt) and his longstanding diagnosis. His primary care physician noted asymmetric cogwheel rigidity on examination and referred him for neurological assessment. He denies exposure to antipsychotic medications, antiemetics, or other dopamine-blocking agents. He denies head trauma, encephalitis, or toxin exposures.

neurological_exam.additional: A low-amplitude, approximately 4-5 Hz resting tremor is present in the right hand, most evident with the patient's hand resting quietly in his lap and during walking; the tremor diminishes with intentional movement and re-emerges after a brief latency on posture holding (re-emergent pattern). When both hands are outstretched, there is a moderate-amplitude bilateral postural and action tremor — more prominent on the left and present since the patient's 40s, consistent with his longstanding tremor history. Glabellar tap sign positive (fails to habituate after 10 taps). Handwriting sample shows early micrographia in the right hand. No myoclonus. Olfactory testing with the University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT): score 28/40, indicating mild hyposmia.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing accurate bilaterally without dysmetria; mild slowing on the right attributable to bradykinesia rather than ataxia. Heel-to-shin intact bilaterally. No cerebellar ataxia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive bilaterally at 3 mm. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus or limitation of vertical gaze. Mild facial hypomimia with mildly reduced spontaneous blink rate. Facial sensation intact. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius 5/5 bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Gait mildly narrow-based with reduced right arm swing; left arm swing preserved. Stride length slightly shortened. En-bloc turning requiring 4 steps. Tandem gait mildly impaired. Pull test: 2 steps of retropulsion with self-correction. No festination or freezing. Rises from chair without arm use but slowly.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented. Speech fluent and of normal volume. Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) 27/30; lost 1 point on serial subtraction and 2 points on delayed recall. No aphasia, apraxia, or neglect.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Increased tone in both upper extremities with clear cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist and elbow, best elicited with activation (contralateral hand opening-closing); mild cogwheel component at the left wrist on reinforcement. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. Bradykinesia evident on right-hand finger tapping with progressive decrement in amplitude and speed after 10 cycles; left hand shows mild slowing but substantially better amplitude maintenance.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, and proprioception intact in all extremities. Vibration mildly reduced at bilateral great toes (age-appropriate). No cortical sensory deficits.
